title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 2
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Reading and Writing · Full practice tests
summary: A complete timed Reading and Writing section — two 32-minute modules, 54 original questions — with an explanation for every answer and your results by skill.

blocks.text: This is a full, original practice version of the Digital SAT **Reading and Writing** section by Mohamed Abdelkriem. It has the same shape as the real section: **two modules of 27 questions**, **32 minutes each**, and every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four answer choices. Some passages include a small table.

rows: Mixed difficulty: easy, medium and hard questions
All 54 questions count toward your practice score

blocks.text: **How the real test differs:** in each real module, 2 of the 27 questions are unscored pretest questions (25 count), and you cannot tell which ones they are, so treat every question seriously. On test day, your performance on Module 1 decides whether you get a harder or an easier Module 2. Here, Module 2 is always the harder version, so a good score on it is a strong sign you are ready.

items: Sit somewhere quiet with no phone, music or notes. Use the built-in timer and do not pause it.
Do Module 1 in one sitting (32 minutes), then Module 2 (32 minutes). In the real test you cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts, so do not go back here either.
Inside a module you may skip and come back, just as you can mark questions for review in the real test. Aim for about 1 minute 10 seconds per question.
Answer every question — there is no penalty for a wrong answer. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can and guess.
Your result is shown as a practice percentage, with results by skill. It is not an official SAT scaled score (200–800).

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
items: اقعد في مكان هادي من غير موبايل، وشغّل التايمر وما توقفهوش.
حل الموديول الأول في 32 دقيقة، وبعدين الموديول التاني في 32 دقيقة. في الامتحان الحقيقي مش هتقدر ترجع للموديول الأول بعد ما تبدأ التاني، فاعمل كده هنا كمان.
جاوب على كل الأسئلة، مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط. لو مش متأكد، شيل الاختيارات الغلط وخمّن.
النتيجة اللي هتظهرلك نسبة مئوية للتدريب بس، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 2
blocks.intro: A full-length Digital SAT Reading and Writing section: two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes per module (54 questions, 64 minutes). In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest questions, and Module 2 adapts to your performance on Module 1 (it is harder or easier). In this practice test all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Questions follow the usual order: Craft and Structure, Information and Ideas, Standard English Conventions, then Expression of Ideas. There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question.

questions.p: Because the light from distant galaxies takes billions of years to reach Earth, astronomers who study these galaxies are, in a sense, looking into the past. The images they collect are not ______ of the galaxies as they exist today but records of how the galaxies appeared long ago.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: predictions
imitations
depictions
rejections
questions.e: The images show the galaxies, but as they were long ago, so they are not "depictions" (pictures) of them as they are today. "Predictions" fails because an image records something that already happened; it does not forecast anything.

questions.p: In parts of West Africa, farmers have long planted rows of cowpeas between rows of millet. The practice is far from ______: cowpeas add nitrogen to the soil and shade the ground, which helps the millet grow and keeps weeds down.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: beneficial
arbitrary
traditional
productive
questions.e: After the colon the text gives clear reasons for the practice, so it is far from "arbitrary" (done without a reason). "Beneficial" and "productive" reverse the meaning, and "traditional" contradicts "have long planted."

questions.p: The composer Hana Okafor rarely writes music that ______ listeners' expectations. Her pieces often begin with a familiar folk melody, but within a few bars the rhythm shifts without warning and the harmony moves into unexpected keys.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: conforms to
disrupts
ignores
outlasts
questions.e: The second sentence shows her music surprising listeners, so she rarely writes music that "conforms to" (follows) their expectations. "Disrupts" and "ignores" are the opposite of what the sentence needs after "rarely" — the classic reversed-meaning trap.

questions.p: Early studies of memory treated forgetting as a simple failure, a sign that stored information had faded away. More recent work views forgetting far more ______: some researchers argue that it helps the brain discard outdated details so that it can apply what it has learned to new situations.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: favorably
dismissively
cautiously
briefly
questions.e: The new view presents forgetting as useful, which is a more positive ("favorable") view than calling it a failure. "Dismissively" would make the new view even more negative, the reverse of what the colon explains.

questions.p: When a thick lava flow cools, it contracts. Because the cooling surface cannot shrink evenly all at once, cracks open in it, and these cracks tend to meet at angles of about 120 degrees, an arrangement that releases stress efficiently. As cooling moves deeper into the flow, the cracks extend downward, dividing the rock into long columns, many of them six-sided. Such columns can be seen at places such as the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It presents a common belief about a rock formation and then shows why that belief is mistaken.
It explains a natural process in stages and then names a place where its results can be seen.
It compares two explanations of how six-sided columns form and then favors one of them.
It describes a famous location in detail and then speculates about how it was formed.
questions.e: The text moves step by step through how cooling lava cracks into columns, then mentions the Giant's Causeway as an example. There is no mistaken belief, no second theory, and no speculation — the location appears only in the last sentence.

questions.p: The station at Harlow Junction had not seen a passenger train in eleven years, yet every morning Mr. Pell unlocked the ticket office, wound the great clock, and swept the platform as though the 7:40 might arrive at any moment. Children from the village sometimes came to watch him work. He never told them why he did it, and after a while they stopped asking, deciding among themselves that the old man simply liked the sound of the broom.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To portray a character's faithful daily routine and suggest that his reasons for it remain private
To explain why passenger trains stopped serving a small village
To describe how the children of a village learned the history of its railway station
To show that a character expects a particular friend to return on the morning train
questions.e: The text focuses on Mr. Pell's careful routine and stresses that he never explains it; the children only guess. It never says why the trains stopped, and no friend is mentioned — that choice adds an idea the text does not support.

questions.p:
Text 1
Many cities have made their buses free to ride, hoping to draw drivers out of their cars. Economist Lena Varga argues that the policy works: in the cities she studied, bus ridership rose by roughly a third within a year of fares being dropped.

Text 2
Studies of free-fare programs consistently report higher ridership, but economist Tomás Ibarra cautions that ridership alone can mislead. In his analysis, most new riders had previously walked or cycled; few car owners changed their habits. Ibarra suggests that frequent, reliable service matters more to drivers than price does.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Ibarra (Text 2) most likely respond to Varga's claim that the policy works?
c: He would agree with her, noting that price is the main factor in drivers' decisions about how to travel.
He would argue that bus ridership did not actually rise in the cities she studied.
He would claim that free fares make bus service less frequent and less reliable.
He would question whether rising ridership shows that the policy reduced driving, since many new riders may not have been drivers.
questions.e: Varga uses higher ridership as proof; Ibarra accepts that ridership rises but says the new riders were mostly walkers and cyclists, not drivers. The "agree" choice reverses his view that service matters more than price, and he never says free fares harm reliability.

questions.p: Lanternfish are small, but they live in enormous numbers. Each night, they swim up from depths of several hundred meters to feed near the surface, then descend again before sunrise. Because they digest their food and release waste in deep water, scientists believe that lanternfish and similar animals move large amounts of carbon from the surface to the deep ocean, playing an important role in how the ocean stores carbon.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Lanternfish feed only in deep water and rarely come near the ocean surface.
Lanternfish are among the largest and most numerous fish in the ocean.
Through their daily journeys up and down, lanternfish likely help carry carbon into the deep ocean.
Scientists have only recently discovered that lanternfish migrate every night.
questions.e: The whole text builds toward the idea that the fish's nightly migration moves carbon downward. The text says they feed near the surface (reversed), calls them small (contradiction), and never says the discovery is recent (unsupported).

questions.p: In 1154, the geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi completed a world map and an accompanying book for Roger II, the Norman king of Sicily. Al-Idrisi did not rely only on older written works. He and his assistants questioned sailors, merchants, and travelers passing through Sicily's busy ports and accepted only the details that several sources agreed on. The result was one of the most accurate descriptions of the known world produced in the twelfth century.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Al-Idrisi's careful way of gathering and checking information helped make his geography unusually accurate for its time.
Roger II traveled widely in order to collect information for al-Idrisi's map.
Al-Idrisi refused to use any older written works when he made his map.
Sicily's ports were the busiest in the twelfth-century Mediterranean world.
questions.e: The text describes al-Idrisi's method (questioning travelers, checking sources) and says it produced an accurate result. "Refused to use any older works" is too extreme — he did not rely ONLY on them. The other choices are unsupported details.

questions.p: Psychologist Rhea Daniels hypothesizes that people remember new information better when they explain it aloud to an imagined listener than when they simply reread it. To test this idea, she gave volunteers a short science article and asked half of them to explain it to an imaginary student and the other half to reread it.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Daniels's hypothesis?
c: Volunteers who reread the article said they felt more confident about the material than volunteers who explained it.
A week later, volunteers who had explained the article recalled more of its key facts than volunteers who had reread it for the same amount of time.
Volunteers who explained the article spent more time on the task than volunteers who reread it.
Volunteers who explained the article to a real person remembered slightly more than those who explained it to an imaginary student.
questions.e: The hypothesis is about memory: explaining should beat rereading. Only the first finding compares memory across those two groups. Confidence and time are not memory, and the real-versus-imaginary listener comparison leaves out rereading entirely.

questions.p:
Meteors counted by the Hillcrest astronomy club
Night | Meteors per hour
August 10 | 18
August 11 | 34
August 12 | 61
August 13 | 29

Members of the Hillcrest astronomy club predicted that this year's meteor shower would reach its peak on August 12. The club's counts support this prediction: ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: the club saw 34 meteors per hour on August 11, nearly twice as many as on August 10.
the club saw fewer meteors per hour on August 13 than on August 11.
the club saw 61 meteors per hour on August 12, more than on any other night it recorded.
the club saw 61 meteors per hour on August 13, its highest count of the shower.
questions.e: A peak on August 12 means August 12 had the highest count, and 61 is the highest number in the table. The other true statements do not involve August 12, and the last choice misreads the table (August 13 had 29).

questions.p:
Wheat test plots, by irrigation method
Method | Water used (thousand liters per plot) | Yield (kilograms per plot)
Flood | 90 | 410
Sprinkler | 65 | 400
Drip | 40 | 395

Agronomist Priya Natarajan concluded that drip irrigation offers the best balance between saving water and keeping yields high. Compared with flood irrigation, drip irrigation ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: used less water and also produced a higher yield.
used less than half as much water while producing a yield only 15 kilograms lower.
used 25 thousand fewer liters of water per plot.
produced the lowest yield of the three methods.
questions.e: Drip used 40 versus 90 thousand liters (less than half) and yielded 395 versus 410 kg (15 kg less): big savings, small loss — a balance. The "higher yield" choice is false, 25 thousand is the drip–sprinkler gap, and "lowest yield" is true but argues against the conclusion.

questions.p: Windcatchers — tall towers built on rooftops in hot, dry parts of Iran — have cooled houses for centuries by catching breezes and directing them into the rooms below. Architect Samir Haddad measured indoor temperatures in two otherwise identical houses in Yazd, one with a working windcatcher and one whose windcatcher had been sealed. On still afternoons, the two houses were equally warm. On breezy afternoons, however, the house with the working windcatcher was several degrees cooler. These results suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: windcatchers cool houses equally well in all kinds of weather.
sealing a windcatcher makes a house warmer than a house built without one.
houses in Yazd are generally warmer on breezy afternoons than on still afternoons.
a windcatcher's cooling effect depends largely on the presence of wind.
questions.e: The cooling difference appeared only when there was a breeze, so the effect depends on wind. "Equally well in all weather" contradicts the still-afternoon result, and no house without a windcatcher was measured.

questions.p: Astronomer Ines Kovač studied a cluster of stars that all formed from the same cloud of gas at about the same time. Because stars that form together begin with nearly identical chemical makeup, Kovač expected their compositions to match closely. Most did, but a few of the stars showed unusually high levels of iron and other heavy elements at their surfaces. Since a star's outer layers can be altered by material that falls onto it, Kovač concluded that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the unusual stars must have formed from a different cloud of gas than the rest of the cluster.
stars that form together usually end up with very different chemical compositions.
the unusual stars may have taken in extra material, such as matter from planets, after they formed.
iron is the most common element at the surface of most stars.
questions.e: The last sentence points to material falling onto a star after birth as the cause. The "different cloud" choice contradicts the premise that all the stars formed from the same cloud, and most stars did match, so "usually very different" is wrong.

questions.p: The oud, a short-necked stringed instrument with a rounded body, is central to much traditional Arab ______ its tone is warm and deep, and because it has no frets, skilled players can slide smoothly between notes that fall outside a Western scale.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: music;
music,
music
music, which
questions.e: Both sides are complete sentences, so a semicolon is needed. A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and "which its tone is" is ungrammatical.

questions.p: The fourteenth-century traveler Ibn Battuta, who set out from Tangier in 1325, spent nearly thirty years on the road and visited many of the great cities of his age, among them Damascus, Syria; Delhi, ______ and Quanzhou, China.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: India,
India:
India
India;
questions.e: SAT/ACT extra rule: when list items already contain commas (city, country), semicolons separate the items. The pattern "Damascus, Syria;" must continue with "Delhi, India;". A comma would blur the items, and a colon cannot appear mid-list.

questions.p: Researchers who study habits often point to one surprising ______ people who seem to have strong self-control do not resist temptation more often than others do; instead, they arrange their lives so that they face fewer temptations in the first place.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: finding,
finding
finding, which
finding:
questions.e: The first part is a complete sentence and what follows explains the "surprising finding," so a colon fits. A comma alone makes a comma splice, no punctuation makes a run-on, and "which" leaves the clause without a proper structure.

questions.p: The Ifugao farmers who first carved rice terraces into the steep mountainsides of the Philippine ______ water from the forests above the fields through a network of channels and bamboo pipes, a system that still irrigates many terraces today.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Cordilleras directed
Cordilleras, directed
Cordilleras; directed
Cordilleras—directed
questions.e: The long subject ("The Ifugao farmers who ... Cordilleras") must flow straight into its verb "directed" with no punctuation. Any comma, semicolon or dash here would wrongly separate the subject from its verb.

questions.p: The Court of the Lions in Granada's Alhambra—named for the twelve marble lions that support its central ______ was built in the fourteenth century under the Nasrid ruler Muhammad V.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: fountain,
fountain;
fountain
fountain—
questions.e: The extra information opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash: dash…dash must match. A comma mixes the pair, a semicolon cuts the subject from its verb "was built," and no punctuation leaves the dash pair unclosed.

questions.p: Each band of rock in the canyon formed from mud, sand, or shells that settled in ancient seas, rivers, or deserts. Taken together, the layers exposed in the canyon walls ______ a record of environmental change stretching back millions of years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: provides
is providing
provide
has provided
questions.e: The subject is the plural noun "layers" ("exposed in the canyon walls" is only a describing phrase), so the plural verb "provide" is needed. "Provides," "is providing" and "has provided" are all singular.

questions.p: A kelp forest is home to hundreds of species of fish, snails, and other animals. When sea otters keep the number of kelp-eating sea urchins in check, the forest grows dense, and ______ canopy can shelter young fish from predators.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: their
it's
they're
its
questions.e: The canopy belongs to "the forest," a singular noun, so the singular possessive "its" is correct. "Their" is plural, and "it's" and "they're" are contractions (it is, they are), not possessives.

questions.p: Founded in 1960 by a group of farmers in a small village, the cooperative now ______ seeds, tools, and storage space among more than two hundred families that grow wheat, lentils, and chickpeas.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: sharing
shares
to share
having shared
questions.e: The sentence needs a main (finite) verb for its subject "the cooperative." "Sharing," "to share" and "having shared" are not finite verbs, so they leave the sentence without a main verb.

questions.p: For centuries, astronomers believed that Saturn was the only planet in the solar system with rings. In 1977, ______ observers watching a star pass behind Uranus saw its light dim briefly several times before and after the planet itself blocked it, a sign that Uranus, too, is circled by rings.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: for example,
however,
similarly,
therefore,
questions.e: The 1977 discovery contradicts the old belief, so a contrast word is needed. "For example" and "similarly" suggest agreement, and "therefore" wrongly presents the discovery as a result of the old belief.

questions.p: Economists call coffee and tea substitutes: when the price of one rises, many shoppers buy more of the other. Printers and ink cartridges are related in a different way. ______ they are complements: because the two are used together, a fall in the price of printers tends to increase sales of ink.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Instead,
Similarly,
For instance,
Nevertheless,
questions.e: The previous sentence says printers and ink are NOT like coffee and tea, and the next sentence says what they are instead. "Similarly" reverses this, "for instance" gives no example of substitutes, and "nevertheless" signals a surprise that does not exist.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Fatima al-Fihri was born in Kairouan, in present-day Tunisia.
• She later settled in Fez, in present-day Morocco.
• In 859 CE, she founded the Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez.
• The Qarawiyyin grew into a major center of learning.
• It is often described as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize how long the Qarawiyyin has existed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Fatima al-Fihri was born in Kairouan, in present-day Tunisia, and later settled in Fez.
The Qarawiyyin, founded by Fatima al-Fihri, grew into a major center of learning.
Founded in 859 CE, the Qarawiyyin in Fez is often described as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
Fatima al-Fihri, the founder of the Qarawiyyin, came from Kairouan in present-day Tunisia.
questions.e: The goal is the institution's long history, so the sentence needs the founding date and the "oldest continuously operating" detail. The other choices focus on the founder's life or on the school's importance, not its age.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Shield volcanoes are formed mainly by runny lava that spreads far before it hardens.
• They have broad, gently sloping sides.
• Mauna Loa in Hawaii is a shield volcano.
• Stratovolcanoes are formed by layers of thick lava and ash.
• They are steep and cone-shaped.
• Mount Fuji in Japan is a stratovolcano.
questions.q: The student wants to contrast the shapes of the two types of volcanoes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Mauna Loa in Hawaii is a shield volcano, and Mount Fuji in Japan is a stratovolcano.
Shield volcanoes are formed by runny lava, while stratovolcanoes are formed by layers of thick lava and ash.
Mount Fuji, a stratovolcano in Japan, is steep and cone-shaped.
While shield volcanoes such as Mauna Loa have broad, gentle slopes, stratovolcanoes such as Mount Fuji are steep and cone-shaped.
questions.e: Only the first choice compares the shapes of both types. The "runny lava" choice is a contrast, but of how the volcanoes form, not their shapes (half-right trap); the others give no contrast of shape.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The spacing effect is the finding that information is remembered better when study is spread out over time.
• It was first described by the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus in the 1880s.
• Ebbinghaus tested his own memory using lists of nonsense syllables.
• Students who study for one hour on each of three days often remember more than students who study for three hours on a single day.
questions.q: The student wants to explain the spacing effect to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The spacing effect was first described by the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus in the 1880s.
The spacing effect—the finding that information is remembered better when study is spread out over time—explains why three one-hour sessions on separate days often beat one three-hour session.
To study memory, Hermann Ebbinghaus tested himself using lists of nonsense syllables.
Students who study for three hours on a single day often remember less than they expect.
questions.e: A reader who has never heard of the spacing effect needs to be told what it is; the first choice defines it and gives a clear example. The Ebbinghaus choices name or describe history without explaining the effect, and the last choice never names or defines it.

questions.p: Mrs. Albright's praise was so ______ that her pupils learned to treasure it: a single word of approval written in the margin of an essay could be the subject of excited conversation in the schoolyard for days.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: effusive
ambiguous
habitual
sparing
questions.e: Pupils treasured her praise because it was rare — "sparing" means given in small amounts. "Effusive" (overflowing) and "habitual" (frequent) would make praise ordinary, the reverse of the text; nothing suggests it was unclear ("ambiguous").

questions.p: Some economists describe the effect of a new factory on a small town as "multiplied": wages paid to workers are spent at local shops, whose owners then hire more staff. Economist Marta Lindqvist considers this account too ______. In her study of twelve towns, much of the new income was spent online or in distant cities, so local gains were far smaller than predicted.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: sanguine
pessimistic
tentative
technical
questions.e: Lindqvist found the real gains smaller than expected, so she thinks the account is too optimistic — "sanguine." "Pessimistic" reverses her point, and nothing suggests the account was too hesitant or too technical.

questions.p: Geologists once assumed that the drifting of continents was far too slow to be measured directly within a human lifetime. Satellite positioning has rendered that assumption ______: instruments can now detect the few centimeters by which some continents shift each year.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: indispensable
plausible
deliberate
untenable
questions.e: Instruments now measure the motion, so the old assumption can no longer be defended — it is "untenable." "Plausible" and "indispensable" would support the assumption the text says was proven wrong.

questions.p: Critics often describe the improvisations of jazz pianist Ruth Abernathy as spontaneous, but her notebooks tell a different story: they contain dozens of versions of the same musical phrases, each one carefully revised. Her apparent ease at the keyboard, the notebooks suggest, was ______.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: effortless
hard-won
accidental
short-lived
questions.e: The notebooks show years of careful revision, so her ease was earned through effort — "hard-won." "Effortless" repeats the critics' view that the text is correcting, and "accidental" is the same trap in another form.

questions.p: In several studies, children who were told that a puzzle measured their intelligence gave up sooner when it became difficult than children who were told it was simply a game. __One explanation is that describing a task as a test of ability turns each mistake into a possible sign of failure rather than a step toward a solution.__ Researchers have also found that this effect weakens when children are reminded that ability grows with practice.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It presents evidence that challenges the finding described in the previous sentence.
It introduces a second finding that is unrelated to the first.
It describes the method researchers used to measure children's intelligence.
It offers a possible reason for the difference in behavior described in the previous sentence.
questions.e: "One explanation is that..." signals a reason for why the first group gave up sooner. It does not challenge the finding, it is clearly related to it, and no method of measuring intelligence is described.

questions.p: Many histories of Gothic architecture name Abbot Suger's rebuilding of the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris, begun in the 1130s, as the starting point of the style. Architectural historian Lucien Morel does not deny the church's importance, but he points out that its pointed arches and ribbed vaults had already appeared, separately, in earlier buildings in Europe and the Islamic world. What Saint-Denis introduced, Morel argues, was not new features but a new way of combining them.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To argue that Saint-Denis had little influence on the buildings that came after it
To describe the construction methods used to build the abbey church of Saint-Denis
To present a scholar's refinement of a common claim about the origins of an architectural style
To explain why pointed arches first appeared in buildings of the Islamic world
questions.e: Morel keeps the common view (Saint-Denis matters) but adjusts it: the church combined existing features rather than inventing them. The "little influence" choice is too extreme — he does not deny its importance — and the other two are side details.

questions.p:
Text 1
Most farmers plow before planting to bury weeds and loosen the soil. Soil scientist Ana Ferreira argues that farmers should stop plowing altogether. Plowing breaks up the soil structure and fungal networks that help fields hold water, and in her long-term trials, unplowed fields lost far less soil during heavy rains.

Text 2
No-till farming clearly benefits soil, but agronomist Kwame Asante notes that its results depend on conditions. In cool, wet regions, unplowed soil can stay cold and waterlogged in spring, delaying planting and lowering yields. There, he recommends reducing plowing rather than giving it up entirely.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Asante (Text 2) most likely respond to Ferreira's recommendation in Text 1?
c: He would accept that not plowing protects soil but argue that giving up plowing entirely may not suit every climate.
He would reject her claim that unplowed fields lose less soil than plowed fields during heavy rains.
He would argue that plowing improves soil structure in cool, wet regions.
He would agree that all farmers should stop plowing, whatever the local conditions.
questions.e: Asante says no-till "clearly benefits soil" (agreeing with her evidence) but warns it can fail in cool, wet regions, so he would object to "stop plowing altogether." He never rejects her data or says plowing improves soil structure.

questions.p: When the letter came, Clara read it twice at the kitchen table and then folded it into a small, precise square, the way her mother had taught her to fold napkins for company. She said nothing to her brother about what it contained. All that afternoon she went about the house finishing tasks that had waited for months—mending the torn curtain in the parlor, oiling the hinge on the garden gate, labeling the jars in the cellar—as if she were preparing the place to be cared for by someone else.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Clara is frustrated that her brother has neglected the household tasks for months.
Clara's mother taught her to keep a tidy and well-organized home.
Clara reacts to the news in a letter by quietly preparing for a change that she does not announce.
Clara decides to ignore the letter and concentrate on her chores instead.
questions.e: Clara keeps the letter secret and readies the house "as if" someone else will look after it, suggesting she is about to leave. The text never blames the brother, the mother detail is minor, and the chores are a response to the letter, not a way of ignoring it.

questions.p: Marine biologist Keiko Tanabe hypothesizes that coral reefs exposed to brief, moderate warming events become more tolerant of later, more severe heat waves, much as a mild challenge can prepare the body for a greater one. She is comparing reefs along a coastline where some sites have experienced moderate warming and others have not.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Tanabe's hypothesis?
c: During a severe heat wave, reefs that had experienced moderate warming two years earlier lost as much coral as nearby reefs that had experienced no earlier warming.
During a severe heat wave, reefs with no history of warming lost more coral than reefs that had experienced moderate warming.
Moderate warming events along the coastline have become more frequent over the past thirty years.
Some reefs lost small amounts of coral during moderate warming events as well as during severe heat waves.
questions.e: If earlier moderate warming made reefs tougher, they should lose less coral; losing the same amount weakens the idea. The "lost more coral" finding supports the hypothesis (reversed trap), and the other two do not compare the two groups of reefs.

questions.p: Paper mills were established in Baghdad in the late eighth century. Historian Yusuf Karimi argues that these mills did more than supply government offices with writing material: by making paper far cheaper than parchment, they allowed the copying and sale of books to spread well beyond the court to scholars, students, and merchants.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Karimi's argument?
c: Government offices in Baghdad switched from parchment to paper for keeping official records.
Paper had been made in China for centuries before the first mills were built in Baghdad.
Ninth-century Baghdad had a large booksellers' market where many shops sold copied works on paper to private buyers.
Parchment continued to be used for some especially valuable copies of important texts.
questions.e: Karimi's claim is that cheap paper spread books to ordinary buyers outside the court; a busy market selling paper books to private buyers shows exactly that. The government-office finding covers only the part he says is NOT the whole story.

questions.p:
Changes after congestion charges were introduced
City | Change in car traffic | Change in bus ridership
Northport | −18% | +11%
Calder | −9% | +4%
Wexley | −22% | +3%
Ashby | −14% | +15%

Economist Dalia Mansour expected that the cities where car traffic fell the most after a congestion charge would also see the largest increases in bus ridership. The data from Wexley, however, do not fit this expectation, since Wexley ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: had an increase in bus ridership of 3%, while Calder had an increase of 4%.
had a smaller decrease in car traffic than Northport did.
had the largest decrease in car traffic of the four cities but the smallest increase in bus ridership.
had both the largest decrease in car traffic and the largest increase in bus ridership.
questions.e: Wexley's traffic fell most (−22%) but its ridership rose least (+3%), the opposite of the expectation. The Calder comparison ignores traffic, and the other two choices misread the table (Northport fell only 18%; Ashby, not Wexley, had the largest ridership rise).

questions.p:
Average words recalled (out of 30), by background condition
Condition | Words recalled
Silence | 17
Instrumental music | 16
Music with lyrics in a language participants did not understand | 15
Music with lyrics in a language participants understood | 11

Psychologists asked participants to memorize a list of words under different background conditions. They concluded that it is mainly understandable words, not music itself, that interfere with memory: ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: participants recalled 16 and 15 words with instrumental music and with lyrics they did not understand, close to the 17 recalled in silence, but only 11 with lyrics they understood.
participants recalled 17 words in silence and 16 words with instrumental music.
participants recalled fewer words in every music condition than they did in silence.
participants recalled 11 words with lyrics they understood, 6 fewer than in silence.
questions.e: The conclusion has two parts: music alone barely hurts recall, and understood words hurt it a lot. Only the first choice shows both. The silence-versus-instrumental choice shows only the first half, and the "fewer in every condition" choice suggests music itself is the problem.

questions.p: Stalagmites grow as dripping water leaves behind thin layers of minerals, and the chemistry of each layer reflects how much rain fell when it formed. Geologist Amara Osei analyzed a stalagmite from a cave in southern Africa and found a band of layers showing an extremely dry period. The band is unusually thin, however, and some layers within it appear to be missing entirely. Osei suggests that the dry period may have lasted longer than the band alone indicates, because ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: wet periods produce thinner mineral layers than dry periods do.
during severe droughts, little or no water may have dripped onto the stalagmite, so few new layers would have formed.
the chemistry of mineral layers cannot reveal how much rain fell in the past.
stalagmites in southern Africa grow faster than stalagmites in other regions.
questions.e: If almost no water dripped during the drought, almost no layers formed, so a thin band could stand for a long time. The "cannot reveal rainfall" choice contradicts the first sentence, and the other two choices do not explain missing layers.

questions.p: Historian Leila Ansari studied letters exchanged by medieval merchants in the Indian Ocean trade. She found that merchants often trusted goods worth large sums to partners in distant ports whom they had never met, usually on the recommendation of a shared associate. Courts rarely enforced the agreements between these partners, yet cases of partners cheating one another appear to have been uncommon. Ansari concludes that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: courts were the main way merchants punished partners who cheated them.
a merchant's reputation within a network of associates was likely a strong check on dishonest behavior.
merchants usually preferred to trade only with members of their own families.
most medieval merchants traveled with their goods to distant ports.
questions.e: Courts rarely acted, yet cheating was rare, and partners were chosen through shared associates — so reputation in the network likely kept people honest. The "courts" choice contradicts the text, and trading with strangers rules out "only family."

questions.p: The deepest known point in the ocean, the Challenger Deep in the western Pacific's Mariana ______ lies nearly 11,000 meters below the sea surface, a depth reached by only a small number of crewed expeditions.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Trench,
Trench;
Trench—
Trench
questions.e: "the Challenger Deep in the western Pacific's Mariana Trench" is extra information opened with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "lies." A dash breaks the matching pair, a semicolon cuts the subject from its verb, and no comma leaves the pair open.

questions.p: The Andromeda Galaxy is moving toward the Milky Way at roughly 110 kilometers per ______ the two galaxies are not expected to collide for about four to five billion years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: second, even so,
second; even so,
second even so,
second, even so;
questions.e: Two complete sentences are joined, and "even so" belongs to the second one, so the semicolon goes before it: "second; even so,". Two commas create a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and putting the semicolon after "even so" attaches the contrast to the wrong clause.

questions.p: In a well-known experiment from the early 1950s, psychologist Solomon Asch asked people to say which of three lines matched a sample line. When the other members of the ______ secretly working with Asch, gave an obviously wrong answer, many participants went along with them.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: group—all of whom were
group, all of whom were
group all of whom were
group; all of whom were
questions.e: "all of whom were secretly working with Asch" is extra information, and it closes with a comma, so it must open with a comma. A dash would not match the closing comma, no punctuation leaves the pair open, and a semicolon cannot introduce a non-sentence.

questions.p: Many gamelan ensembles of Java and Bali are made up mainly of tuned bronze percussion ______ hanging gongs, metallophones with bronze keys, and rows of small kettle-shaped gongs. Players traditionally learn their parts by ear rather than from written notation.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: instruments;
instruments, such as:
instruments:
instruments that are:
questions.e: A complete sentence introduces a list, so a colon is right. A semicolon cannot introduce a list, and a colon after "such as" or "that are" is wrong because those words leave the sentence incomplete before the colon.

questions.p: The yearly migration of humpback whales between cold feeding grounds near the poles and warm breeding waters near the equator, one of the longest journeys made by any mammal, ______ thousands of kilometers in each direction.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: cover
have covered
are covering
covers
questions.e: The subject is the singular noun "migration"; "of humpback whales," the place names and the long appositive in commas are all interruptions. So the singular verb "covers" is needed. The plural options agree with "whales," the classic nearest-noun trap.

questions.p: Mimar Sinan served as chief architect of the Ottoman Empire for about fifty years and designed hundreds of buildings, from bridges and baths to grand mosques. Completed in 1557 after seven years of construction, ______
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Sinan designed the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul as one of his best-known works.
Sinan's best-known works include the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul.
visitors still consider the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul one of Sinan's best-known works.
the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul is one of Sinan's best-known works.
questions.e: The modifier "Completed in 1557 after seven years of construction" must sit right next to the thing that was completed: the mosque. The other choices place Sinan, his works, or visitors next to the modifier — dangling modifiers.

questions.p: The agricultural scientist Norman Borlaug spent years breeding wheat that could resist disease and produce more grain. By the time he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970, the high-yield varieties he developed ______ harvests in Mexico, India, and Pakistan.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: will transform
are transforming
had already transformed
transform
questions.e: "By the time ... received ... in 1970" points to an action completed before another past event, which calls for the past perfect "had already transformed." The future and present forms clash with the past time frame.

questions.p: Behavioral economists have found that many ______ decisions about saving for retirement are strongly shaped by default options: when enrollment in a company savings plan is automatic, far more workers take part than when they must sign up themselves.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: employees'
employee's
employees
employees's
questions.e: "Many" requires a plural, and the decisions belong to the employees, so the plural possessive "employees'" is right. "Employee's" is singular, "employees" has no possessive, and "employees's" is not a correct form.

questions.p: Most meteorites that reach Earth are pieces of asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter. A small number, ______ have chemical signatures that match rocks collected on the Moon, which suggests they were blasted off the lunar surface by impacts and later fell to Earth.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: for instance,
therefore,
however,
likewise,
questions.e: Lunar meteorites are an exception to the general rule that most come from asteroids, so a contrast is needed. "For instance" and "likewise" treat them as part of the same group, and "therefore" invents a cause-and-effect link.

questions.p: In many traditional markets, prices are set by bargaining rather than printed on tags. Bargaining takes time, and it can leave buyers unsure whether they paid a fair price. ______ it allows sellers to adjust prices to each customer and gives loyal customers a chance to be rewarded with better deals.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Thus,
Still,
Similarly,
In other words,
questions.e: The text moves from the drawbacks of bargaining to its advantages, so a concession word like "Still" fits. "Thus" presents the advantages as caused by the drawbacks, and "similarly" and "in other words" suggest the second point repeats the first.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi was a tenth-century Persian astronomer.
• In about 964 CE, he completed the Book of Fixed Stars.
• The book described the positions, brightness, and colors of hundreds of stars.
• It contains the earliest known written record of the Andromeda Galaxy, which al-Sufi called a “small cloud.”
• Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize the importance of al-Sufi's observation of Andromeda. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The Andromeda Galaxy, which al-Sufi observed, is about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.
Al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars described the positions, brightness, and colors of hundreds of stars.
Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi, a tenth-century Persian astronomer, completed the Book of Fixed Stars in about 964 CE.
Al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars, completed in about 964 CE, contains the earliest known written record of the Andromeda Galaxy, which he called a “small cloud.”
questions.e: "Earliest known written record" is what makes the observation important, and only the first choice includes it. The distance fact is true but says nothing about the observation's importance, and the other two never mention Andromeda.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Agronomist Grace Mwangi wanted to know whether strips of wildflowers planted beside crop fields reduce pest damage.
• She worked with twenty farms in Kenya.
• Ten farms planted wildflower strips; ten did not.
• Wildflowers attract insects, such as parasitic wasps, that attack crop pests.
• Farms with wildflower strips had 30% less pest damage.
questions.q: The student wants to describe how Mwangi's study was carried out. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Mwangi found that farms with wildflower strips had 30% less pest damage than farms without them.
Wildflowers attract parasitic wasps and other insects that attack crop pests.
To test whether wildflower strips reduce pest damage, Mwangi compared twenty Kenyan farms, ten of which planted strips beside their fields and ten of which did not.
Mwangi wanted to know whether wildflower strips planted beside fields reduce pest damage.
questions.e: "How the study was carried out" means its method: twenty farms, ten with strips and ten without. The 30% choice gives the result, the wasp choice gives background, and the last choice gives only the research question.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Bioluminescence is light produced by living things through a chemical reaction.
• Many deep-sea anglerfish use a glowing lure to attract prey.
• Some squid release clouds of glowing fluid to confuse predators.
• Certain shrimp produce light on their undersides that matches the faint light from above, hiding their outline from predators below.
questions.q: The student wants to make a generalization about how ocean animals use bioluminescence. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Ocean animals use bioluminescence in different ways, including to attract prey, to confuse predators, and to hide from them.
Many deep-sea anglerfish use a glowing lure to attract prey.
Bioluminescence is light produced by living things through a chemical reaction.
Some squid release glowing fluid, and certain shrimp produce light on their undersides.
questions.e: A generalization sums up the pattern across the examples: animals use light to hunt, to escape and to hide. The anglerfish and squid–shrimp choices give specific cases, not a general statement, and the definition does not mention uses at all.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for EVERY question — including the ones you got right. A lucky guess is not a skill yet.
For each mistake, write down the skill tag and the trap you fell for (reversed meaning, too extreme, half-right, comma splice, nearest-noun agreement, and so on).

List your two or three weakest skills from the results by skill, and go back to the matching lessons: Words in Context; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences.

For grammar mistakes, review Sentence Boundaries; Commas and Extra Information; Colons, Dashes and Semicolons; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronouns; Verb Tense, Aspect and Finiteness; Modifiers, Parallel Structure and Comparisons; Plurals and Possessives. For the last questions of each module, review Transitions and Rhetorical Synthesis.
If you ran out of time, reread Time Strategy and How to Attack Every Question. Then wait a few days and take Practice Test 3 under the same timed conditions.
